Beyond Comparing Measures

This chapter leaves the setting of scalar measures on a common ambient space. Vector- and matrix-valued OT transports mass with internal degrees of freedom, Gromov--Wasserstein compares metric-measure spaces without a prescribed correspondence, and quantum OT replaces scalar couplings by positive operators. In each case, the transport plan must also encode structure carried by the support, the fibers, or the non-commutative state space.

Guiding Comparison

Classical OT compares two scalar measures through a ground cost. Vector- and matrix-valued OT keeps the base space but enriches the mass attached to each point. Gromov--Wasserstein removes the common base space and compares internal distances. Quantum OT keeps the marginal idea but replaces vectors and matrices of masses by positive operators and partial traces.

Vector and Matrix-Valued Measures¶

Scalar OT transports a nonnegative density. In imaging, color processing, spectral analysis, diffusion tensor imaging and quantum-inspired models, the object attached to a point can instead have several nonnegative components or a positive semidefinite matrix. The first step beyond scalar OT is the positive vector-valued case: the fiber remains linear and commutative, but the transport cost may couple its channels.

Positive Vector-Valued Measures¶

The simplest way to keep internal structure in transport is to attach several nonnegative masses to each spatial point and to decide whether these channels move independently or interact through the cost.

Definition: Positive Vector-Valued Measure

A positive R+m\RR_+^mR+m​-valued measure on X\XX is a tuple

α=(α1,…,αm)∈M+(X;R+m),\al=(\al^1,\ldots,\al^m)\in\mathcal M_+(\X;\RR_+^m),α=(α1,…,αm)∈M+​(X;R+m​),
(1)

where each component αk\al^kαk is a nonnegative finite measure.

This models multi-channel densities such as color histograms, spectral bins or several species transported on the same domain. In a conservative model the mass of each channel is preserved, so one assumes α0k(X)=α1k(X)\al_0^k(\X)=\al_1^k(\X)α0k​(X)=α1k​(X) for every kkk. The natural vector-valued extension therefore starts from the positive cone R+m\RR_+^mR+m​.

For the dynamic formulas below, assume that X\XX is either Rd\RR^dRd, the flat torus, or a bounded convex domain in Rd\RR^dRd equipped with no-flux boundary conditions. First suppose that the endpoints and the curve have densities. The direct analogue of Benamou--Brenier fixes a vector density ut(x)∈R+mu_t(x)\in\RR_+^mut​(x)∈R+m​ and a spatial flux Vt(x)=(Vt,1,…,Vt,d)∈(Rm)dV_t(x)=(V_{t,1},\ldots,V_{t,d})\in(\RR^m)^dVt​(x)=(Vt,1​,…,Vt,d​)∈(Rm)d, where Vt,ℓkV_{t,\ell}^kVt,ℓk​ is the momentum of channel kkk in spatial direction ℓ\ellℓ. The conservative vector transport cost associated with an action density Φ\PhiΦ is

WΦ2(α0,α1):=inf⁡u,V∫01 ⁣∫XΦ(ut(x),Vt(x))  dx  dt\mathcal W_{\Phi}^2(\al_0,\al_1) \eqdef \inf_{u,V} \int_0^1\!\int_\X \Phi(u_t(x),V_t(x))\,\d x\,\d tWΦ2​(α0​,α1​):=u,Vinf​∫01​∫X​Φ(ut​(x),Vt​(x))dxdt
(2)

subject to the endpoint constraints u0 dx=α0u_0\d x=\al_0u0​dx=α0​, u1 dx=α1u_1\d x=\al_1u1​dx=α1​ and the componentwise continuity equation

∂tut+∇x⋅Vt=0,(∇x⋅Vt)k=∑ℓ=1d∂xℓVt,ℓk.\partial_t u_t+\nabla_x\cdot V_t=0, \qquad (\nabla_x\cdot V_t)^k = \sum_{\ell=1}^d\partial_{x_\ell}V_{t,\ell}^k.∂t​ut​+∇x​⋅Vt​=0,(∇x​⋅Vt​)k=ℓ=1∑d​∂xℓ​​Vt,ℓk​.
(3)

Thus each component satisfies its own continuity equation, but the cost may still couple the components. Singular curves are handled as in scalar dynamic OT by replacing densities and fluxes by measures and using the lower semicontinuous perspective recession convention.

A simple quadratic family is obtained from a mobility matrix M(u)∈S+m\mathsf M(u)\in\mathbb S_+^mM(u)∈S+m​:

ΦM(u,V)=∑ℓ=1dVℓ⊤M(u)†Vℓ,\Phi_{\mathsf M}(u,V) = \sum_{\ell=1}^d V_\ell^\top \mathsf M(u)^\dagger V_\ell,ΦM​(u,V)=ℓ=1∑d​Vℓ⊤​M(u)†Vℓ​,
(4)

with the usual convention that the value is finite only when each VℓV_\ellVℓ​ belongs to the range of M(u)\mathsf M(u)M(u). If u↦M(u)u\mapsto\mathsf M(u)u↦M(u) is linear and takes values in S+m\mathbb S_+^mS+m​, this action is jointly convex and positively one-homogeneous in (u,V)(u,V)(u,V). Indeed, the matrix fractional map (M,z)↦z⊤M†z(M,z)\mapsto z^\top M^\dagger z(M,z)↦z⊤M†z is jointly convex on its effective domain, and M(su)=sM(u)\mathsf M(su)=s\mathsf M(u)M(su)=sM(u) for s>0s>0s>0. For m=1m=1m=1 and M(u)=u\mathsf M(u)=uM(u)=u, one recovers exactly the scalar Benamou--Brenier action. For

Mdiag(u)=diag⁡(u1,…,um),\mathsf M_{\mathrm{diag}}(u)=\operatorname{diag}(u_1,\ldots,u_m),Mdiag​(u)=diag(u1​,…,um​),

the channels move independently. Non-diagonal mobilities are the simplest way to couple the coordinates while keeping the same componentwise conservation law. For instance, with q=m−1/2(1,…,1)q=m^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)q=m−1/2(1,…,1) and κ≥0\kappa\geq0κ≥0,

Proposition: Diagonal Positive Vector Benamou--Brenier

Assume that α0k,α1k∈M+(X)\al_0^k,\al_1^k\in\mathcal M_+(\X)α0k​,α1k​∈M+​(X) have finite second moments and the same mass mkm_kmk​ for every kkk. For the diagonal mobility Mdiag\mathsf M_{\mathrm{diag}}Mdiag​,

Wdiag2(α0,α1)=∑k:mk>0mk W22 ⁣(α0kmk,α1kmk),\mathcal W_{\mathrm{diag}}^2(\al_0,\al_1) = \sum_{k:m_k>0} m_k\, \Wass_2^2\!\left( \frac{\al_0^k}{m_k}, \frac{\al_1^k}{m_k} \right),Wdiag2​(α0​,α1​)=k:mk​>0∑​mk​W22​(mk​α0k​​,mk​α1k​​),

with the convention that zero-mass channels contribute zero.

The conservative positive-cone model above is the basic extension of Benamou--Brenier. Adding a source term ∂tu+∇⋅V=S\partial_t u+\nabla\cdot V=S∂t​u+∇⋅V=S and a convex perspective penalty in SSS gives unbalanced or reaction--transport variants Maas et al., 2015Maas et al., 2016Dolbeault et al., 2009Mielke, 2013. These generalized transport models include dissipation and density modulation. The endpoints are two-mode mixtures: at each spatial mode the two channels have Gaussian profiles with the same center but different amplitudes.

Positive Matrix-Valued Measures¶

The next simplest fiber is the positive matrix cone. This is the simplest tensor-valued model beyond vectors: the diagonal entries behave like positive channels, while the eigenvectors encode local orientations.

Definition: Positive Matrix-Valued Measure

Write Sm\mathbb S^mSm for real symmetric matrices and S+m\mathbb S_+^mS+m​ for the positive semidefinite cone. A positive S+m\mathbb S_+^mS+m​-valued measure is a countably additive map from Borel sets of X\XX to S+m\mathbb S_+^mS+m​; the cone of such measures is denoted by

A∈M+(X;S+m).\mathcal A\in\mathcal M_+(\X;\mathbb S_+^m).A∈M+​(X;S+m​).
(9)

Equivalently, A\mathcal AA is a symmetric matrix of finite signed measures such that A(E)⪰0\mathcal A(E)\succeq0A(E)⪰0 for every Borel set EEE. If A\mathcal AA has density A(x)⪰0A(x)\succeq0A(x)⪰0, then tr⁡A(x)\operatorname{tr}A(x)trA(x) is the scalar amount of mass at xxx, while, wherever tr⁡A(x)>0\operatorname{tr}A(x)>0trA(x)>0, the normalized matrix A(x)/tr⁡A(x)A(x)/\operatorname{tr}A(x)A(x)/trA(x) records an internal covariance or orientation. This is the matrix analogue of the positive vector case: diagonal matrices encode nonnegative vector components, and non-diagonal matrices add a local eigenbasis.

The conservative Benamou--Brenier model fixes a matrix density At(x)∈S+mA_t(x)\in\mathbb S_+^mAt​(x)∈S+m​ and symmetric matrix fluxes Pt(x)=(Pt,1,…,Pt,d)∈(Sm)dP_t(x)=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,d})\in(\mathbb S^m)^dPt​(x)=(Pt,1​,…,Pt,d​)∈(Sm)d. With no flux through the boundary of X\XX, the full matrix mass ∫XAt(x) dx\int_\X A_t(x)\d x∫X​At​(x)dx is conserved, so the endpoints must have the same total matrix. The model minimizes the matrix-perspective action

Wmat2(A0,A1):=inf⁡A,P∫01 ⁣∫X∑ℓ=1dtr⁡ ⁣(Pt,ℓ⊤At†Pt,ℓ) dx  dt\mathcal W_{\mathrm{mat}}^2(\mathcal A_0,\mathcal A_1) \eqdef \inf_{A,P} \int_0^1\!\int_\X \sum_{\ell=1}^d \operatorname{tr}\!\left(P_{t,\ell}^{\top} A_t^\dagger P_{t,\ell}\right) \d x\,\d tWmat2​(A0​,A1​):=A,Pinf​∫01​∫X​ℓ=1∑d​tr(Pt,ℓ⊤​At†​Pt,ℓ​)dxdt
(10)

subject to A0 dx=A0A_0\d x=\mathcal A_0A0​dx=A0​, A1 dx=A1A_1\d x=\mathcal A_1A1​dx=A1​ and to the matrix-valued continuity equation

∂tAt+∇x⋅Pt=0,∇x⋅Pt=∑ℓ=1d∂xℓPt,ℓ.\partial_t A_t+\nabla_x\cdot P_t=0, \qquad \nabla_x\cdot P_t = \sum_{\ell=1}^d\partial_{x_\ell}P_{t,\ell}.∂t​At​+∇x​⋅Pt​=0,∇x​⋅Pt​=ℓ=1∑d​∂xℓ​​Pt,ℓ​.
(11)

Here A†A^\daggerA† denotes the Moore--Penrose inverse, with the usual lower-semicontinuous perspective convention: the action is finite only when the columns of each Pt,ℓP_{t,\ell}Pt,ℓ​ belong to the range of AtA_tAt​. The matrix fractional map (A,P)↦tr⁡(P⊤A†P)(A,P)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(P^\top A^\dagger P)(A,P)↦tr(P⊤A†P) is jointly convex on this effective domain and positively one-homogeneous in (A,P)(A,P)(A,P). This gives the simplest non-trivial matrix-valued transport model: spatial motion is conservative, but the fiber carries orientation through the eigenvectors of At(x)A_t(x)At​(x).

Proposition: Diagonal Matrix Subproblem

Assume that the endpoints are diagonal in a fixed orthonormal basis,

Ai=diag⁡(αi1,…,αim),i=0,1,\mathcal A_i=\operatorname{diag}(\al_i^1,\ldots,\al_i^m), \qquad i=0,1,Ai​=diag(αi1​,…,αim​),i=0,1,
(12)

and that α0k(X)=α1k(X)=mk\al_0^k(\X)=\al_1^k(\X)=m_kα0k​(X)=α1k​(X)=mk​ for every kkk. If one restricts the admissible curves in (10) to remain diagonal in that basis,

At=diag⁡(ut1,…,utm),Pt,ℓ=diag⁡(Vt,ℓ1,…,Vt,ℓm),A_t=\operatorname{diag}(u_t^1,\ldots,u_t^m), \qquad P_{t,\ell}=\operatorname{diag}(V_{t,\ell}^1,\ldots,V_{t,\ell}^m),At​=diag(ut1​,…,utm​),Pt,ℓ​=diag(Vt,ℓ1​,…,Vt,ℓm​),
(13)

then the restricted matrix problem has value

∑k:mk>0mk W22 ⁣(α0kmk,α1kmk).\sum_{k:m_k>0} m_k\, \Wass_2^2\!\left( \frac{\al_0^k}{m_k}, \frac{\al_1^k}{m_k} \right).k:mk​>0∑​mk​W22​(mk​α0k​​,mk​α1k​​).
(14)

with zero contribution from zero-mass channels. Thus the commuting matrix submodel is exactly the diagonal positive vector-valued Benamou--Brenier model.

Proof

The continuity equation (11) is diagonal entry by diagonal entry and gives ∂tuk+∇⋅Vk=0\partial_t u^k+\nabla\cdot V^k=0∂t​uk+∇⋅Vk=0. Moreover,

∑ℓ=1dtr⁡ ⁣(Pt,ℓ⊤At†Pt,ℓ)=∑k=1m∣Vtk∣2utk,\sum_{\ell=1}^d \operatorname{tr}\!\left(P_{t,\ell}^{\top}A_t^\dagger P_{t,\ell}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^m\frac{|V_t^k|^2}{u_t^k},ℓ=1∑d​tr(Pt,ℓ⊤​At†​Pt,ℓ​)=k=1∑m​utk​∣Vtk​∣2​,
(15)

with the same scalar perspective convention as before. The admissible set and the action are therefore exactly those of the diagonal vector model.

The restriction to a fixed diagonal basis gives eigenvalue transport; it should be read as a commuting submodel, not as a claim that non-diagonal excursions can never change the unrestricted value. The genuinely matrix-valued case starts when the eigenspaces vary with xxx or along the interpolation, so that the transported object carries both mass and orientation. Static matrix-valued Monge--Kantorovich problems and dual test-function metrics were developed in Ning & Georgiou, 2014Jiang et al., 2012Ning et al., 2015; dynamic versions and related non-commutative geometries appear in Chen et al., 2016Chen et al., 2020Carlen & Maas, 2014Peyré et al., 2019. The figure below shows the analogous independent/coupled contrast for positive 2×22\times22×2 matrix fibers, using two localized matrix modes whose eigenvalue profiles share a common center at each mode.

Wasserstein Over Wasserstein¶

The construction can be iterated. Once (X,d)(\X,d)(X,d) is a metric space, the set of probability measures on X\XX becomes a metric space through Wp\Wass_pWp​. It can therefore serve as a new ground space. This is useful whenever the objects to compare are themselves random probability measures, or mixtures whose components are meaningful objects rather than only a collapsed density.

The standard setting is that of Polish spaces, introduced in Definition: Polish Metric Space. These assumptions provide separability, completeness, tightness criteria and regular conditional probabilities. The next proposition shows that Wasserstein spaces preserve this well-behaved structure.

Proposition: Wasserstein Spaces As Ground Spaces

Let 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty1≤p<∞. If (X,d)(\X,d)(X,d) is Polish, then (Pp(X),Wp)(\Pp_p(\X),\Wass_p)(Pp​(X),Wp​) is Polish. If X\XX is compact, then Pp(X)=P(X)\Pp_p(\X)=\Pp(\X)Pp​(X)=P(X) and this space is compact for Wp\Wass_pWp​. Consequently, the construction may be iterated, with the corresponding finite-moment condition at every level.

Proof

From a Wp\Wass_pWp​-Cauchy sequence, extract a subsequence (αk)k(\alpha_k)_k(αk​)k​ such that ∑kWp(αk,αk+1)<∞\sum_k\Wass_p(\alpha_k,\alpha_{k+1})<\infty∑k​Wp​(αk​,αk+1​)<∞. Gluing optimal couplings of consecutive terms produces random variables (Xk)k(X_k)_k(Xk​)k​ with laws αk\alpha_kαk​ and ∑k∥d(Xk,Xk+1)∥Lp<∞\sum_k\|d(X_k,X_{k+1})\|_{L^p}<\infty∑k​∥d(Xk​,Xk+1​)∥Lp​<∞. Hence (Xk)k(X_k)_k(Xk​)k​ converges almost surely and in LpL^pLp to an X\XX-valued random variable, whose law is the Wp\Wass_pWp​ limit. Separability follows by approximating measures with finitely supported measures on a countable dense subset and rational weights. If X\XX is compact, Prokhorov compactness and Wasserstein metrization of weak convergence give compactness.

Fix 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty1≤p<∞. Elements of Pp(Pp(X))\Pp_p(\Pp_p(\X))Pp​(Pp​(X)) are probability laws over probability measures, or random probability measures. A measurable parametric family gives

A=(ζ↦αζ)♯γ.\mathfrak A=(\zeta\mapsto\alpha_\zeta)_\sharp\gamma.A=(ζ↦αζ​)♯​γ.
(19)

This law belongs to Pp(Pp(X))\Pp_p(\Pp_p(\X))Pp​(Pp​(X)) precisely when, for one and hence every x0∈Xx_0\in\Xx0​∈X,

∫Wp(αζ,δx0)p  dγ(ζ)<∞.\int \Wass_p(\alpha_\zeta,\delta_{x_0})^p\,\d\gamma(\zeta)<\infty.∫Wp​(αζ​,δx0​​)pdγ(ζ)<∞.
(20)

For A∈P(P(X))\mathfrak A\in\Pp(\Pp(\X))A∈P(P(X)), the collapsed mixture is defined by

∫Xf(x) dαˉA(x)=∫P(X)(∫Xf(x) dα(x)) dA(α)\int_\X f(x)\d\bar\alpha_{\mathfrak A}(x) = \int_{\Pp(\X)} \left(\int_\X f(x)\d\alpha(x)\right) \d\mathfrak A(\alpha)∫X​f(x)dαˉA​(x)=∫P(X)​(∫X​f(x)dα(x))dA(α)

for every bounded continuous fff.

∫Xd(x,x0)p  dαˉA(x)=∫Pp(X)Wp(α,δx0)p  dA(α).\int_\X d(x,x_0)^p\,\d\bar\alpha_{\mathfrak A}(x) = \int_{\Pp_p(\X)}\Wass_p(\alpha,\delta_{x_0})^p\,\d\mathfrak A(\alpha).∫X​d(x,x0​)pdαˉA​(x)=∫Pp​(X)​Wp​(α,δx0​​)pdA(α).
(22)

The Wasserstein distance on the Wasserstein space is

Wpp(A,B):=inf⁡Π∈Π(A,B)∫Pp(X)×Pp(X)Wpp(α,β) dΠ(α,β),A,B∈Pp(Pp(X)).\mathbb W_p^p(\mathfrak A,\mathfrak B) \eqdef \inf_{\Pi\in\Couplings(\mathfrak A,\mathfrak B)} \int_{\Pp_p(\X)\times\Pp_p(\X)} \Wass_p^p(\alpha,\beta)\d\Pi(\alpha,\beta), \qquad \mathfrak A,\mathfrak B\in\Pp_p(\Pp_p(\X)).Wpp​(A,B):=Π∈Π(A,B)inf​∫Pp​(X)×Pp​(X)​Wpp​(α,β)dΠ(α,β),A,B∈Pp​(Pp​(X)).
(23)

For p=2p=2p=2, Gaussian mixtures provide an explicit example with two geometries. A mixture can be viewed as a collapsed density on X\XX, or as a component law over Gaussian atoms in the Bures--Wasserstein space. For two component laws

A=∑iaiδN(mi,Σi),B=∑jbjδN(nj,Λj),\mathfrak A=\sum_i a_i\delta_{\Gaussian(m_i,\Sigma_i)}, \qquad \mathfrak B=\sum_j b_j\delta_{\Gaussian(n_j,\Lambda_j)},A=i∑​ai​δN(mi​,Σi​)​,B=j∑​bj​δN(nj​,Λj​)​,
(24)

the component-level problem uses the cost

Cij=∥mi−nj∥2+B(Σi,Λj)2.C_{ij}=\norm{m_i-n_j}^2+\Bb(\Sigma_i,\Lambda_j)^2.Cij​=∥mi​−nj​∥2+B(Σi​,Λj​)2.
(25)

If Π⋆\Pi^\starΠ⋆ is an optimal coupling between the weights aaa and bbb, and if AijA_{ij}Aij​ is the Brenier linear part from Σi\Sigma_iΣi​ to Λj\Lambda_jΛj​, each active pair follows the Gaussian geodesic

mij,t=(1−t)mi+tnj,Σij,t=((1−t)Id+tAij)Σi((1−t)Id+tAij)⊤.m_{ij,t}=(1-t)m_i+t n_j, \qquad \Sigma_{ij,t} = \big((1-t)\Id+tA_{ij}\big)\Sigma_i \big((1-t)\Id+tA_{ij}\big)^\top.mij,t​=(1−t)mi​+tnj​,Σij,t​=((1−t)Id+tAij​)Σi​((1−t)Id+tAij​)⊤.
(26)

Collapsing these component geodesics gives

αˉt=∑i,jΠij⋆N(mij,t,Σij,t).\bar\alpha_t= \sum_{i,j}\Pi^\star_{ij}\Gaussian(m_{ij,t},\Sigma_{ij,t}).αˉt​=i,j∑​Πij⋆​N(mij,t​,Σij,t​).
(27)

This component-level interpolation generally differs from the true W2\Wass_2W2​ interpolation between the collapsed mixture densities.

show_book_figure("kantorovich-wow-mixtures")

Two interpolations between the same asymmetric three-component one-dimensional Gaussian mixtures. The red endpoint has a broad central component carrying most of the mass, while the blue endpoint has two dominant sharp side modes. Proposition: Collapsing Is Non-Expansive

Let (X,d)(\X,d)(X,d) be Polish, let 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty1≤p<∞, and let A,B∈Pp(Pp(X))\mathfrak A,\mathfrak B\in\Pp_p(\Pp_p(\X))A,B∈Pp​(Pp​(X)). Then

Wp(αˉA,βˉB)≤Wp(A,B).\Wass_p(\bar\alpha_{\mathfrak A},\bar\beta_{\mathfrak B}) \leq \mathbb W_p(\mathfrak A,\mathfrak B).Wp​(αˉA​,βˉ​B​)≤Wp​(A,B).
(28)
Proof

Fix a coupling Π\PiΠ between A\mathfrak AA and B\mathfrak BB and η>0\eta>0η>0. A measurable-selection theorem gives a measurable kernel πα,β∈Π(α,β)\pi_{\alpha,\beta}\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)πα,β​∈Π(α,β) whose cost is at most Wp(α,β)p+η\Wass_p(\alpha,\beta)^p+\etaWp​(α,β)p+η. Integrating this kernel against Π\PiΠ gives a coupling between the collapsed mixtures. Its cost is at most the Π\PiΠ-average of Wpp(α,β)\Wass_p^p(\alpha,\beta)Wpp​(α,β) plus η\etaη. Letting η↓0\eta\downarrow0η↓0, taking the infimum over Π\PiΠ, and then taking the ppp-th root proves the claim.

This viewpoint also clarifies lower bounds for Gromov--Wasserstein distances: a metric-measure space can be mapped to a law of local distance profiles, and these laws can be compared by Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein.

Remark: Local profiles as Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein laws

Given a metric-measure space X=(X,dX,αX)\XX=(\X,\dist_\X,\al_\X)X=(X,dX​,αX​), each point defines a local distance distribution

αx=(dX(x,⋅))♯αX∈P(R+),DX=(x↦αx)♯αX∈P(P(R+)).\alpha_x=(\dist_\X(x,\cdot))_\sharp\al_\X\in\Pp(\RR_+), \qquad \mathfrak D_\XX=(x\mapsto\alpha_x)_\sharp\al_\X\in\Pp(\Pp(\RR_+)).αx​=(dX​(x,⋅))♯​αX​∈P(R+​),DX​=(x↦αx​)♯​αX​∈P(P(R+​)).
(29)

The Memoli profile lower bound in Proposition Proposition: Memoli Profile Lower Bound is precisely a Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein comparison of these laws of local profiles. It replaces the full pairwise distortion by an ordinary OT problem whose ground cost is itself a one-dimensional Wasserstein distance.

Gromov--Wasserstein¶

Gromov--Wasserstein compares spaces through their internal distance structures rather than through a fixed ambient ground cost. This is the right extension for graphs, shapes and point clouds whose points are not pre-aligned.

Discrete Formulation¶

Optimal transport needs a ground cost CCC to compare histograms (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), and thus cannot be used directly if the histograms are not defined on the same underlying space, or if one cannot pre-register these spaces to define a ground cost. Instead, assume that two matrices D∈Rn×nD\in\RR^{n\times n}D∈Rn×n and D′∈Rm×mD'\in\RR^{m\times m}D′∈Rm×m represent relationships between points. A typical scenario is when these matrices are powers of distance matrices. Define the quadratic distortion and its minimum by

ED,D′(P):=∑i,j,i′,j′Δ(Di,i′,Dj,j′′)pPi,jPi′,j′,GW⁡((a,D),(b,D′))p:=min⁡P∈U(a,b)ED,D′(P).\begin{aligned} \mathcal E_{D,D'}(P) &\eqdef \sum_{i,j,i',j'} \Delta(D_{i,i'},D'_{j,j'})^pP_{i,j}P_{i',j'}, \\ \operatorname{GW}((a,D),(b,D'))^p &\eqdef \min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)}\mathcal E_{D,D'}(P). \end{aligned}ED,D′​(P)GW((a,D),(b,D′))p​:=i,j,i′,j′∑​Δ(Di,i′​,Dj,j′′​)pPi,j​Pi′,j′​,:=P∈U(a,b)min​ED,D′​(P).​
(30)

where p≥1p\geq1p≥1 and Δ\DeltaΔ is usually Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣\Delta(u,v)=|u-v|Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣. This is a non-convex quadratic problem over the transport polytope. In the uniform case with m=nm=nm=n and PPP constrained to be a permutation matrix, it becomes a Quadratic Assignment Problem, already NP-hard in full generality Loiola et al., 2007. The relaxed coupling formulation can therefore be read as a soft graph-matching model Lyzinski et al., 2016.

show_book_figure("gromov-isometry-matching")

Gromov--Wasserstein correspondences under increasing deformation. The red and blue point clouds are not compared through an ambient Euclidean cross-cost; instead, the GW coupling compares their internal pairwise distances. A perfectly isometric copy admits a clean structural match, while mild and deliberately stronger deformations progressively bend the correspondence.

The interactive demo uses a fixed structural correspondence and lets the deformation change the pairwise-distance residual. This isolates the quantity minimized by the GW objective.

Interactive panel. Use the deformation and point controls to inspect correspondences when only within-space distances are meaningful.

When D,D′D,D'D,D′ are genuine distance matrices, the construction below defines a distance between metric spaces equipped with a probability distribution, up to measure-preserving isometries Mémoli, 2011Sturm, 2012Schmitzer & Schnörr, 2013. The same construction also explains why GW satisfies the triangle inequality after quotienting by isometries, and its relation to Hausdorff and Gromov--Hausdorff distances is discussed at the end of the section.

General Setting¶

The continuous formulation abstracts the discrete distance matrices into metric-measure spaces, so that GW compares intrinsic geometries independently of labels, parametrizations or ambient coordinates.

Definition: Metric-Measure Space

A metric-measure space is a triple

X=(X,dX,α),\mathbb X=(\X,d_\X,\alpha),X=(X,dX​,α),
(31)

where (X,dX)(\X,d_\X)(X,dX​) is Polish and α\alphaα is a Borel probability measure on X\XX. For a finite ppp-Gromov--Wasserstein distance one assumes

∫X×XdX(x,x′)p  dα(x) dα(x′)<∞.\int_{\X\times\X}d_\X(x,x')^p\,\d\alpha(x)\d\alpha(x')<\infty.∫X×X​dX​(x,x′)pdα(x)dα(x′)<∞.
(32)

Compactness is often assumed below to avoid additional tightness and integrability arguments.

For metric-measure spaces X=(X,dX,α)\mathbb X=(\X,d_\X,\alpha)X=(X,dX​,α) and Y=(Y,dY,β)\mathbb Y=(\Y,d_\Y,\beta)Y=(Y,dY​,β), define

GW⁡(X,Y)p:=min⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫X2×Y2Δ(dX(x,x′),dY(y,y′))p dπ(x,y) dπ(x′,y′).\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y)^p \eqdef \min_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int_{\X^2\times\Y^2} \Delta(d_\X(x,x'),d_\Y(y,y'))^p \d\pi(x,y)\d\pi(x',y').GW(X,Y)p:=π∈Π(α,β)min​∫X2×Y2​Δ(dX​(x,x′),dY​(y,y′))pdπ(x,y)dπ(x′,y′).
(33)
Proposition: Fixed-Space GW Is Controlled by Wasserstein

Let α,β∈Pp(X)\alpha,\beta\in\Pp_p(\X)α,β∈Pp​(X) be probability measures on the same metric space (X,dX)(\X,d_\X)(X,dX​), and take Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣\Delta(u,v)=|u-v|Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣ in (33). Then

GW⁡((X,dX,α),(X,dX,β))≤2Wp(α,β).\operatorname{GW}((\X,d_\X,\alpha),(\X,d_\X,\beta)) \leq 2\Wass_p(\alpha,\beta).GW((X,dX​,α),(X,dX​,β))≤2Wp​(α,β).
(34)

The Wasserstein distance uses the same ground metric dXd_\XdX​. The factor two comes from the normalization in (33).

Proof

Let π\piπ be any coupling between α\alphaα and β\betaβ. For two independent pairs (X,Y),(X′,Y′)∼π(X,Y),(X',Y')\sim\pi(X,Y),(X′,Y′)∼π, the reverse triangle inequality gives

∣dX(X,X′)−dX(Y,Y′)∣≤dX(X,Y)+dX(X′,Y′).\left|d_\X(X,X')-d_\X(Y,Y')\right| \leq d_\X(X,Y)+d_\X(X',Y').∣dX​(X,X′)−dX​(Y,Y′)∣≤dX​(X,Y)+dX​(X′,Y′).
(35)

Taking the LpL^pLp norm and using Minkowski gives a bound by 2(∫dX(x,y)p dπ)1/p2(\int d_\X(x,y)^p\d\pi)^{1/p}2(∫dX​(x,y)pdπ)1/p. Optimizing over π\piπ proves the claim.

Definition: Isometric Metric-Measure Spaces

Two metric-measure spaces X=(X,dX,α)\mathbb X=(\X,d_\X,\alpha)X=(X,dX​,α) and Y=(Y,dY,β)\mathbb Y=(\Y,d_\Y,\beta)Y=(Y,dY​,β) are isometric if there exists a bijection ϕ:supp⁡(α)→supp⁡(β)\phi:\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\to\operatorname{supp}(\beta)ϕ:supp(α)→supp(β) such that ϕ♯α=β\phi_\sharp\alpha=\betaϕ♯​α=β and

dY(ϕ(x),ϕ(x′))=dX(x,x′)d_\Y(\phi(x),\phi(x'))=d_\X(x,x')dY​(ϕ(x),ϕ(x′))=dX​(x,x′)
(36)

for all x,x′∈supp⁡(α)x,x'\in\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)x,x′∈supp(α).

Theorem: Gromov--Wasserstein Metric Modulo Isometries

For compact metric-measure spaces, p≥1p\geq1p≥1 and Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣\Delta(u,v)=|u-v|Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣, GW⁡\operatorname{GW}GW defines a distance up to measure-preserving isometries.

Proof

Compactness makes the coupling set compact and the distortion continuous, so an optimal coupling exists. A measure-preserving isometry induces a graph coupling with zero distortion; symmetry and non-negativity are immediate.

If GW⁡(X,Y)=0\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y)=0GW(X,Y)=0 and π\piπ is optimal, then dX(x,x′)=dY(y,y′)d_\X(x,x')=d_\Y(y,y')dX​(x,x′)=dY​(y,y′) holds π⊗π\pi\otimes\piπ⊗π-almost everywhere. By continuity, this equality holds on supp⁡(π)2\operatorname{supp}(\pi)^2supp(π)2. Both X\mathbb XX and Y\mathbb YY are isometric to the support space (supp⁡(π),dπ,π)(\operatorname{supp}(\pi),d_\pi,\pi)(supp(π),dπ​,π), where

dπ((x,y),(x′,y′)):=12dX(x,x′)+12dY(y,y′).d_\pi((x,y),(x',y')) \eqdef \frac12d_\X(x,x')+\frac12d_\Y(y,y').dπ​((x,y),(x′,y′)):=21​dX​(x,x′)+21​dY​(y,y′).
(37)

The first projection is measure-preserving and distance-preserving on supp⁡(π)\operatorname{supp}(\pi)supp(π), and compactness gives surjectivity onto supp⁡(α)\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)supp(α); the same argument applies to the second projection.

For the triangle inequality, glue optimal couplings between X,Y\mathbb X,\mathbb YX,Y and between Y,Z\mathbb Y,\mathbb ZY,Z. The projected X×Z\X\times\ZX×Z marginal is feasible, and the pointwise triangle inequality together with Minkowski gives

GW⁡(X,Z)≤GW⁡(X,Y)+GW⁡(Y,Z).\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Z) \leq \operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y) + \operatorname{GW}(\mathbb Y,\mathbb Z).GW(X,Z)≤GW(X,Y)+GW(Y,Z).
(38)

This proves the triangle inequality and completes the metric proof.

Proposition: Marginal Stability and Empirical GW Rates

Let X=(X,dX,α)\mathbb X=(\X,d_\X,\alpha)X=(X,dX​,α) and Y=(Y,dY,β)\mathbb Y=(\Y,d_\Y,\beta)Y=(Y,dY​,β) be compact metric-measure spaces. Replacing the marginals by α~\widetilde\alphaα and β~\widetilde\betaβ​ gives

∣GW⁡((X,dX,α~),(Y,dY,β~))−GW⁡(X,Y)∣≤2WpX(α~,α)+2WpY(β~,β).\left| \operatorname{GW}((\X,d_\X,\widetilde\alpha),(\Y,d_\Y,\widetilde\beta)) - \operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y) \right| \leq 2\Wass_p^\X(\widetilde\alpha,\alpha) + 2\Wass_p^\Y(\widetilde\beta,\beta).∣∣​GW((X,dX​,α),(Y,dY​,β​))−GW(X,Y)∣∣​≤2WpX​(α,α)+2WpY​(β​,β).
(39)

Consequently, for empirical measures α^n\widehat\alpha_nαn​ and β^m\widehat\beta_mβ​m​,

E∣GW⁡((X,dX,α^n),(Y,dY,β^m))−GW⁡(X,Y)∣≤2EWpX(α^n,α)+2EWpY(β^m,β).\mathbb E\left| \operatorname{GW}((\X,d_\X,\widehat\alpha_n),(\Y,d_\Y,\widehat\beta_m)) - \operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y) \right| \leq 2\mathbb E\Wass_p^\X(\widehat\alpha_n,\alpha) + 2\mathbb E\Wass_p^\Y(\widehat\beta_m,\beta).E∣∣​GW((X,dX​,αn​),(Y,dY​,β​m​))−GW(X,Y)∣∣​≤2EWpX​(αn​,α)+2EWpY​(β​m​,β).
(40)
Proof

Apply the GW triangle inequality in both directions. Each error term compares the same underlying metric space equipped with two different measures, so Proposition: Fixed-Space GW Is Controlled by Wasserstein bounds it by twice the corresponding ordinary Wasserstein distance. Taking expectations yields the empirical bound; the rates are therefore those developed in Sample Complexity.

The metric structure also gives geodesics. Sturm’s construction allows one to speak about interpolation, barycenters and gradient flows directly on the space of metric-measure spaces, even though the intermediate space lives on a product support and is therefore expensive numerically Sturm, 2012.

Proposition: Gromov--Wasserstein Geodesics

Let X0=(X0,dX0,α0)\mathbb X_0=(\X_0,d_{\X_0},\alpha_0)X0​=(X0​,dX0​​,α0​) and X1=(X1,dX1,α1)\mathbb X_1=(\X_1,d_{\X_1},\alpha_1)X1​=(X1​,dX1​​,α1​) be compact metric-measure spaces, and let π⋆\pi^\starπ⋆ be an optimal coupling. Define, on Z=X0×X1\mathcal Z=\X_0\times\X_1Z=X0​×X1​,

dt((x0,x1),(x0′,x1′)):=(1−t)dX0(x0,x0′)+tdX1(x1,x1′),Xt=(Z,dt,π⋆).d_t((x_0,x_1),(x'_0,x'_1)) \eqdef (1-t)d_{\X_0}(x_0,x'_0) + t d_{\X_1}(x_1,x'_1), \qquad \mathbb X_t=(\mathcal Z,d_t,\pi^\star).dt​((x0​,x1​),(x0′​,x1′​)):=(1−t)dX0​​(x0​,x0′​)+tdX1​​(x1​,x1′​),Xt​=(Z,dt​,π⋆).
(41)

For 0<t<10<t<10<t<1, dtd_tdt​ is a metric. At the endpoints one quotients the product space by the corresponding zero-distance relation. Then t↦Xtt\mapsto\mathbb X_tt↦Xt​ is a constant-speed geodesic:

GW⁡(Xs,Xt)=∣t−s∣GW⁡(X0,X1).\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X_s,\mathbb X_t) = |t-s|\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X_0,\mathbb X_1).GW(Xs​,Xt​)=∣t−s∣GW(X0​,X1​).
(42)
Proof

For s<ts<ts<t, couple Xs\mathbb X_sXs​ and Xt\mathbb X_tXt​ by the diagonal coupling on Z\mathcal ZZ. The distance difference is exactly

dt(z,z′)−ds(z,z′)=(t−s)(dX1(x1,x1′)−dX0(x0,x0′)),d_t(z,z')-d_s(z,z') = (t-s)\big(d_{\X_1}(x_1,x'_1)-d_{\X_0}(x_0,x'_0)\big),dt​(z,z′)−ds​(z,z′)=(t−s)(dX1​​(x1​,x1′​)−dX0​​(x0​,x0′​)),
(43)

so GW⁡(Xs,Xt)≤(t−s)D\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X_s,\mathbb X_t)\leq(t-s)DGW(Xs​,Xt​)≤(t−s)D, where D=GW⁡(X0,X1)D=\operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X_0,\mathbb X_1)D=GW(X0​,X1​). Applying the triangle inequality to X0,Xs,Xt,X1\mathbb X_0,\mathbb X_s,\mathbb X_t,\mathbb X_1X0​,Xs​,Xt​,X1​ gives the reverse bound.

Proposition: Memoli Profile Lower Bound

Let X=(X,dX,α)\mathbb X=(\X,d_\X,\alpha)X=(X,dX​,α) and Y=(Y,dY,β)\mathbb Y=(\Y,d_\Y,\beta)Y=(Y,dY​,β) be compact metric-measure spaces. For each x∈Xx\in\Xx∈X and y∈Yy\in\Yy∈Y, define the distance-profile measures on R+\RR_+R+​ by

αx:=(dX(x,⋅))♯α,βy:=(dY(y,⋅))♯β.\alpha_x\eqdef(d_\X(x,\cdot))_\sharp\alpha, \qquad \beta_y\eqdef(d_\Y(y,\cdot))_\sharp\beta.αx​:=(dX​(x,⋅))♯​α,βy​:=(dY​(y,⋅))♯​β.
(44)

Let DX=(x↦αx)♯α\mathfrak D_\mathbb X=(x\mapsto\alpha_x)_\sharp\alphaDX​=(x↦αx​)♯​α and DY=(y↦βy)♯β\mathfrak D_\mathbb Y=(y\mapsto\beta_y)_\sharp\betaDY​=(y↦βy​)♯​β. Then

Wp(DX,DY)≤GW⁡(X,Y),\mathbb W_p(\mathfrak D_\mathbb X,\mathfrak D_\mathbb Y) \leq \operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y),Wp​(DX​,DY​)≤GW(X,Y),
(45)

where Wp\mathbb W_pWp​ is the Wasserstein-over-Wasserstein distance (23), whose ground metric is the one-dimensional Wp\Wass_pWp​ distance between profile measures.

Proof

Fix any π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β). It induces a coupling (x,y)↦(αx,βy)(x,y)\mapsto(\alpha_x,\beta_y)(x,y)↦(αx​,βy​) between the profile laws, hence

Wp(DX,DY)p≤∫X×YWp(αx,βy)p  dπ(x,y).\mathbb W_p(\mathfrak D_\mathbb X,\mathfrak D_\mathbb Y)^p \leq \int_{\X\times\Y} \Wass_p(\alpha_x,\beta_y)^p\,\d\pi(x,y).Wp​(DX​,DY​)p≤∫X×Y​Wp​(αx​,βy​)pdπ(x,y).
(46)

For fixed (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), the map (x′,y′)↦(dX(x,x′),dY(y,y′))(x',y')\mapsto(d_\X(x,x'),d_\Y(y,y'))(x′,y′)↦(dX​(x,x′),dY​(y,y′)) pushes the same coupling π\piπ to a coupling between αx\alpha_xαx​ and βy\beta_yβy​. Integrating the resulting one-dimensional OT bound over (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) gives the GW objective for π\piπ. Taking the infimum over π\piπ proves the claim.

The next figure exposes the two nested transport problems on densely sampled silhouettes: sorting each distance row computes the one-dimensional profile costs exactly, then an outer assignment couples the resulting empirical profile laws.

# Exact sorted profiles; the histograms are display summaries only.
show_book_figure("gromov-memoli-distance-profiles")

Mémoli distance profiles expose a computable lower bound for intrinsic GW comparison. The cat and bunny silhouettes are discretized by 300 well-spread farthest-point samples and normalized to unit diameter. Eight representative cat anchors are selected by a second farthest-point pass; their bunny partners are their exact images under the optimal profile assignment with cost Cij=W22(αxi,βyj)C_{ij}=\Wass_2^2(\alpha_{x_i},\beta_{y_j})Cij​=W22​(αxi​​,βyj​​). Matching colors identify each pair, its segment and its two side histograms. The 20 histogram bins are used only for display: every profile cost is computed exactly by sorting all 300 distances. The value below the shapes is the certified Mémoli lower bound.

This lower bound is useful computationally because the profile cost matrix Cij=Wp(αxi,βyj)pC_{ij}=\Wass_p(\alpha_{x_i},\beta_{y_j})^pCij​=Wp​(αxi​​,βyj​​)p is an ordinary OT cost between points. Solving this easier OT problem gives a geometry-aware initialization for the non-convex GW iterations.

Relation With Wasserstein-Procrustes¶

The profile lower bound is intrinsic. In Euclidean applications, it is naturally paired with an extrinsic upper certificate obtained by registering the two measures before applying the ordinary Wasserstein distance.

Proposition: Wasserstein-Procrustes Upper Certificate

Let α,β\alpha,\betaα,β be probability measures on Rd\RR^dRd, equipped with the Euclidean distance, and take Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣\Delta(u,v)=|u-v|Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣. If Wp,E(d)\Wass_{p,\mathrm E(d)}Wp,E(d)​ denotes the quotient Wasserstein distance under the Euclidean group, then

GW⁡((Rd,∥⋅∥,α),(Rd,∥⋅∥,β))≤2 Wp,E(d)([α],[β]).\operatorname{GW}((\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\alpha),(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\beta)) \leq 2\,\Wass_{p,\mathrm E(d)}([\alpha],[\beta]).GW((Rd,∥⋅∥,α),(Rd,∥⋅∥,β))≤2Wp,E(d)​([α],[β]).
(47)
Proof

Let g,h∈E(d)g,h\in\mathrm E(d)g,h∈E(d) be rigid motions. They preserve all pairwise Euclidean distances, so (Rd,∥⋅∥,α)(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\alpha)(Rd,∥⋅∥,α) is isometric to (Rd,∥⋅∥,g♯α)(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},g_\sharp\alpha)(Rd,∥⋅∥,g♯​α), and similarly for β\betaβ and h♯βh_\sharp\betah♯​β. Hence GW⁡\operatorname{GW}GW is unchanged by pushing the two measures forward by ggg and hhh. Applying Proposition: Fixed-Space GW Is Controlled by Wasserstein to g♯αg_\sharp\alphag♯​α and h♯βh_\sharp\betah♯​β gives

GW⁡((Rd,∥⋅∥,α),(Rd,∥⋅∥,β))≤2 Wp(g♯α,h♯β).\operatorname{GW}((\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\alpha),(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\beta)) \leq 2\,\Wass_p(g_\sharp\alpha,h_\sharp\beta).GW((Rd,∥⋅∥,α),(Rd,∥⋅∥,β))≤2Wp​(g♯​α,h♯​β).
(48)

Taking the infimum over g,h∈E(d)g,h\in\mathrm E(d)g,h∈E(d) proves the result.

Wasserstein-Procrustes therefore gives an extrinsic certificate that a Euclidean GW distance is small. The converse need not hold, because a small GW value may be achieved by an intrinsic correspondence that is not induced by any ambient rigid motion. Combining the profile lower bound with the Procrustes upper certificate gives the sandwich

Wp(DX,DY)≤GW⁡(X,Y)≤2 Wp,E(d)([α],[β]),\mathbb W_p(\mathfrak D_\mathbb X,\mathfrak D_\mathbb Y) \leq \operatorname{GW}(\mathbb X,\mathbb Y) \leq 2\,\Wass_{p,\mathrm E(d)}([\alpha],[\beta]),Wp​(DX​,DY​)≤GW(X,Y)≤2Wp,E(d)​([α],[β]),
(49)

where X=(Rd,∥⋅∥,α)\mathbb X=(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\alpha)X=(Rd,∥⋅∥,α) and Y=(Rd,∥⋅∥,β)\mathbb Y=(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\beta)Y=(Rd,∥⋅∥,β). The left term is intrinsic and inexpensive; the right term is an ambient rigid-registration certificate.

Entropic Regularization and Fused GW¶

For the common squared distortion Δ(u,v)2=(u−v)2\Delta(u,v)^2=(u-v)^2Δ(u,v)2=(u−v)2, one often seeks a stationary point of the entropic relaxation

min⁡P∈U(a,b)ED,D′(P)−ϵH(P).\min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)} \mathcal E_{D,D'}(P)-\epsilon H(P).P∈U(a,b)min​ED,D′​(P)−ϵH(P).
(50)

For symmetric distance matrices, define the half-gradient

C(P):=D⊙2a 1m⊤+1n(D′⊙2b)⊤−2D P D′⊤,∇ED,D′(P)=2C(P).\C(P) \eqdef D^{\odot2}a\,\mathbf 1_m^\top + \mathbf 1_n(D'^{\odot2}b)^\top - 2D\,P\,D'^\top, \qquad \nabla\mathcal E_{D,D'}(P)=2\C(P).C(P):=D⊙2a1m⊤​+1n​(D′⊙2b)⊤−2DPD′⊤,∇ED,D′​(P)=2C(P).
(51)

A standard fixed-point linearization Peyré et al., 2016 computes

P(ℓ+1)=argmin⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨P,C(P(ℓ))⟩−ϵ2H(P).P^{(\ell+1)} = \operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)} \langle P,\C(P^{(\ell)})\rangle -\frac{\epsilon}{2}H(P).P(ℓ+1)=P∈U(a,b)argmin​⟨P,C(P(ℓ))⟩−2ϵ​H(P).
(52)

The factor ϵ/2\epsilon/2ϵ/2 is essential because C(P)\C(P)C(P) is one half of the quadratic gradient. Each update is an ordinary entropic OT problem and can therefore be solved with Sinkhorn iterations. If the iterates converge to a positive fixed point, it satisfies the stationarity conditions of the regularized GW objective. The basic fixed-point iteration is not a descent method in general and has no global guarantee for this non-convex problem; line searches or proximal variants are needed when monotone decrease is required.

Fused Gromov--Wasserstein augments the structural term with a feature transport cost Vayer et al., 2019. In the discrete case, given a cross-feature cost M∈Rn×mM\in\RR^{n\times m}M∈Rn×m and a parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]λ∈[0,1], one minimizes

FGW⁡λ,p((a,D),(b,D′))p:=min⁡P∈U(a,b)(1−λ)∑i,jMijPij+λ∑i,j,i′,j′Δ(Dii′,Djj′′)pPijPi′j′.\operatorname{FGW}_{\lambda,p}((a,D),(b,D'))^p \eqdef \min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)} (1-\lambda)\sum_{i,j}M_{ij}P_{ij} + \lambda \sum_{i,j,i',j'} \Delta(D_{ii'},D'_{jj'})^pP_{ij}P_{i'j'}.FGWλ,p​((a,D),(b,D′))p:=P∈U(a,b)min​(1−λ)i,j∑​Mij​Pij​+λi,j,i′,j′∑​Δ(Dii′​,Djj′′​)pPij​Pi′j′​.
(53)

The endpoints λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 recover feature-only OT and pure GW respectively; intermediate values trade attribute matching against structural matching. The first term compares node attributes in the usual OT sense, and the second compares intrinsic geometry; this is useful when two spaces have both distances and features, and the two sources of information may disagree.

Hausdorff and Gromov--Hausdorff Viewpoints¶

If A,BA,BA,B are compact subsets of a common metric space (Z,dZ)(\mathcal Z,d_\mathcal Z)(Z,dZ​), their Hausdorff distance is

dHZ(A,B)=max⁡{sup⁡a∈Ainf⁡b∈BdZ(a,b),sup⁡b∈Binf⁡a∈AdZ(a,b)}.d_{\mathrm H}^{\mathcal Z}(A,B) = \max\left\{ \sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}d_\mathcal Z(a,b), \sup_{b\in B}\inf_{a\in A}d_\mathcal Z(a,b) \right\}.dHZ​(A,B)=max{a∈Asup​b∈Binf​dZ​(a,b),b∈Bsup​a∈Ainf​dZ​(a,b)}.
(54)

The Gromov--Hausdorff distance removes the common ambient space by minimizing this quantity over all isometric embeddings into a third space:

dGH(X,Y)=inf⁡Z,ϕ,ψdHZ(ϕ(X),ψ(Y)).d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\X,\Y) = \inf_{\mathcal Z,\phi,\psi} d_{\mathrm H}^{\mathcal Z}(\phi(\X),\psi(\Y)).dGH​(X,Y)=Z,ϕ,ψinf​dHZ​(ϕ(X),ψ(Y)).
(55)

Equivalently, it is half the minimal distortion of a correspondence between X\XX and Y\YY Gromov, 2001Mémoli, 2007. This is a worst-case set distance: every point must be matched with small distortion. Gromov--Wasserstein replaces correspondences by probability couplings and worst-case distortion by averaged distortion. It is therefore better adapted to noisy sampled shapes and weighted graphs, but it can ignore small sets of mass that would dominate the Hausdorff distance.

Algorithm: Entropic Gromov--Wasserstein linearization

Input: Symmetric metric matrices D,D′\distD,\distD'D,D′, weights a,b\a,\ba,b, regularization ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol, maximum iterations LLL.

Output: Approximate entropic GW coupling P∈U(a,b)\P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)P∈U(a,b).

Initialize: Set P(0)=a⊗b\P^{(0)}=\a\otimes\bP(0)=a⊗b.

For k=0,…,L−1k=0,\ldots,L-1k=0,…,L−1 do:

C(k)=D⊙2a 1m⊤+1n(D′⊙2b)⊤−2D P(k) D′⊤.\C^{(k)} = \distD^{\odot2}\a\,\ones_m^\top + \ones_n(\distD'^{\odot2}\b)^\top - 2\distD\,\P^{(k)}\,\transp{\distD'}.C(k)=D⊙2a1m⊤​+1n​(D′⊙2b)⊤−2DP(k)D′⊤.

Solve entropic OT subproblem: P(k+1)=arg min⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨P,C(k)⟩−(ϵ/2)H(P).\P^{(k+1)} = \uargmin{\P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)} \dotp{\P}{\C^{(k)}}-(\epsilon/2)\HD(\P).P(k+1)=argminP∈U(a,b)​⟨P,C(k)⟩−(ϵ/2)H(P).

If ∥P(k+1)−P(k)∥F≤tol\norm{\P^{(k+1)}-\P^{(k)}}_{\mathrm F}\leq\mathrm{tol}∥∥​P(k+1)−P(k)∥∥​F​≤tol then:

Return P(k+1)\P^{(k+1)}P(k+1).

Return P(L)\P^{(L)}P(L).

Example: Application to structured objects

Graphs, molecules, meshes and point clouds often do not come with a common coordinate system or a reliable node-to-node correspondence. GW compares them through their internal distances, so the coupling Pij\P_{ij}Pij​ becomes a soft structural correspondence rather than a spatial displacement. This is useful for graph matching, node embedding, shape comparison and molecule or mesh alignment Peyré et al., 2016Vayer et al., 2019. When node attributes are also available, fused GW below adds a feature transport term to the intrinsic distortion, separating what should be preserved as structure from what should be matched as signal.

Example: Application to multi-omics alignment

Multi-omics experiments can produce unmatched point clouds in different feature spaces, for instance RNA and ATAC profiles measured on different cells. If direct feature comparison is unavailable or incomplete, the relational term in GW preserves neighborhood structure; if partial cross-feature information exists, fused GW uses it through MijM_{ij}Mij​. Unbalanced and co-optimal variants further allow the number and relative importance of cells or features to differ across modalities. The mathematical template is therefore precise: preserve within-modality geometry while learning a cross-modality coupling Tran et al., 2022Ryu et al., 2024Stanojevic et al., 2022.

Quantum Optimal Transport¶

Quantum optimal transport replaces probability vectors by density matrices and scalar couplings by positive operators on a tensor product space. This is the right language when the transported objects are matrix-valued signals, covariance-like descriptors or quantum states, and it exposes a precise bridge between OT, non-commutative entropy and operator scaling Ning & Georgiou, 2014Chen et al., 2016Chen et al., 2020Peyré et al., 2019Caglioti et al., 2020Chakrabarti et al., 2019.

Finite-Dimensional States and Couplings¶

Definition: Hermitian and Density Matrices

Let Hn\mathbb H_nHn​ be the real vector space of n×nn\times nn×n Hermitian matrices,

Hn+={A∈Hn:A⪰0},Hn+,1={A∈Hn+:tr⁡(A)=1}.\mathbb H_n^+ = \{A\in\mathbb H_n:A\succeq0\}, \qquad \mathbb H_n^{+,1} = \{A\in\mathbb H_n^+:\operatorname{tr}(A)=1\}.Hn+​={A∈Hn​:A⪰0},Hn+,1​={A∈Hn+​:tr(A)=1}.
(56)

Elements of Hn+,1\mathbb H_n^{+,1}Hn+,1​ are density matrices.

A joint quantum state between Cn\mathbb C^nCn and Cm\mathbb C^mCm is a matrix T∈Hnm+T\in\mathbb H_{nm}^+T∈Hnm+​ acting on Cn⊗Cm\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^mCn⊗Cm. Its marginals are the partial traces, defined by duality through

tr⁡(F Tr⁡BT)=tr⁡((F⊗Im)T),tr⁡(G Tr⁡AT)=tr⁡((In⊗G)T).\operatorname{tr}(F\,\operatorname{Tr}_B T) = \operatorname{tr}((F\otimes I_m)T), \qquad \operatorname{tr}(G\,\operatorname{Tr}_A T) = \operatorname{tr}((I_n\otimes G)T).tr(FTrB​T)=tr((F⊗Im​)T),tr(GTrA​T)=tr((In​⊗G)T).
(57)

for all F∈HnF\in\mathbb H_nF∈Hn​ and G∈HmG\in\mathbb H_mG∈Hm​. Thus Tr⁡B(T)∈Hn+\operatorname{Tr}_B(T)\in\mathbb H_n^+TrB​(T)∈Hn+​ and Tr⁡A(T)∈Hm+\operatorname{Tr}_A(T)\in\mathbb H_m^+TrA​(T)∈Hm+​ play exactly the role of the two marginals of a classical coupling.

Definition: Finite-Dimensional Quantum OT

Let A∈Hn+,1A\in\mathbb H_n^{+,1}A∈Hn+,1​, B∈Hm+,1B\in\mathbb H_m^{+,1}B∈Hm+,1​ and let C∈HnmC\in\mathbb H_{nm}C∈Hnm​ be a Hermitian cost observable. The quantum OT value is the semidefinite program

QOT⁡C(A,B):=min⁡T∈Hnm+{tr⁡(CT):Tr⁡B(T)=A, Tr⁡A(T)=B}.\operatorname{QOT}_C(A,B) \eqdef \min_{T\in\mathbb H_{nm}^+} \left\{ \operatorname{tr}(CT): \operatorname{Tr}_B(T)=A,\ \operatorname{Tr}_A(T)=B \right\}.QOTC​(A,B):=T∈Hnm+​min​{tr(CT):TrB​(T)=A, TrA​(T)=B}.
(58)

The feasible set is never empty, since A⊗BA\otimes BA⊗B has marginals AAA and BBB.

Example: Classical diagonal case

Suppose that AAA, BBB and CCC are diagonal in fixed product bases. Let ΔA\Delta_AΔA​ and ΔB\Delta_BΔB​ be the corresponding dephasing maps. For every feasible TTT, the matrix T~=(ΔA⊗ΔB)(T)\widetilde T=(\Delta_A\otimes\Delta_B)(T)T=(ΔA​⊗ΔB​)(T) is positive, has the same partial traces, and satisfies tr⁡(CT~)=tr⁡(CT)\operatorname{tr}(C\widetilde T)=\operatorname{tr}(CT)tr(CT)=tr(CT). Hence an optimizer may be chosen diagonal. Its diagonal entries form a nonnegative matrix with the prescribed row and column sums, so (58) reduces exactly to classical Kantorovich OT. Non-commuting data may instead require off-diagonal coherences or entanglement.

Proposition: Quantum Kantorovich Duality

For A∈Hn+,1A\in\mathbb H_n^{+,1}A∈Hn+,1​ and B∈Hm+,1B\in\mathbb H_m^{+,1}B∈Hm+,1​, the dual of (58) is

QOT⁡C(A,B)=sup⁡F∈Hn, G∈Hm{tr⁡(FA)+tr⁡(GB):F⊗Im+In⊗G⪯C}.\operatorname{QOT}_C(A,B) = \sup_{F\in\mathbb H_n,\ G\in\mathbb H_m} \left\{ \operatorname{tr}(FA)+\operatorname{tr}(GB) : F\otimes I_m+I_n\otimes G\preceq C \right\}.QOTC​(A,B)=F∈Hn​, G∈Hm​sup​{tr(FA)+tr(GB):F⊗Im​+In​⊗G⪯C}.
(59)

There is no duality gap. If A,BA,BA,B are positive definite, the supremum is attained. For singular marginals, the primal reduces to the tensor product of their supports; on this reduced space the corresponding dual maximum is attained, while the full-space formula is always valid as a supremum.

Proof

Introduce Hermitian Lagrange multipliers FFF and GGG for the two marginal constraints. Using (57), the Lagrangian is

tr⁡(FA)+tr⁡(GB)+tr⁡ ⁣((C−F⊗Im−In⊗G)T).\operatorname{tr}(FA)+\operatorname{tr}(GB) + \operatorname{tr}\!\left((C-F\otimes I_m-I_n\otimes G)T\right).tr(FA)+tr(GB)+tr((C−F⊗Im​−In​⊗G)T).
(60)

Minimizing over T⪰0T\succeq0T⪰0 gives a finite lower bound if and only if C−F⊗Im−In⊗G⪰0C-F\otimes I_m-I_n\otimes G\succeq0C−F⊗Im​−In​⊗G⪰0, in which case the infimum in TTT is 0. When A,B≻0A,B\succ0A,B≻0, the coupling A⊗BA\otimes BA⊗B is strictly feasible, so Slater’s theorem gives equality of primal and dual values and dual attainment.

For singular marginals, let PA,PBP_A,P_BPA​,PB​ be their support projections. Positivity and

tr⁡ ⁣(((In−PA)⊗Im)T)=tr⁡((In−PA)A)=0\operatorname{tr}\!\left(((I_n-P_A)\otimes I_m)T\right) = \operatorname{tr}((I_n-P_A)A)=0tr(((In​−PA​)⊗Im​)T)=tr((In​−PA​)A)=0
(61)

imply T=(PA⊗PB)T(PA⊗PB)T=(P_A\otimes P_B)T(P_A\otimes P_B)T=(PA​⊗PB​)T(PA​⊗PB​). Thus the primal is exactly the problem compressed to supp⁡(A)⊗supp⁡(B)\operatorname{supp}(A)\otimes\operatorname{supp}(B)supp(A)⊗supp(B), where both reduced marginals are positive definite and Slater applies. The unreduced dual values approach this reduced maximum by choosing sufficiently negative potentials on the orthogonal complements.

The dual potentials have the usual scalar gauge freedom: replacing (F,G)(F,G)(F,G) by (F+tIn,G−tIm)(F+tI_n,G-tI_m)(F+tIn​,G−tIm​) leaves both the constraint and the value unchanged because tr⁡(A)=tr⁡(B)=1\operatorname{tr}(A)=\operatorname{tr}(B)=1tr(A)=tr(B)=1.

Entropic Regularization and Bregman Iterations¶

Definition: von Neumann Quantum Entropy

For a density matrix or positive semidefinite matrix TTT, the shifted von Neumann entropy functional used here is

H(T)=tr⁡ ⁣(T(log⁡T−I)),∇H(T)=log⁡T,H(T) = \operatorname{tr}\!\left(T(\log T-I)\right), \qquad \nabla H(T)=\log T,H(T)=tr(T(logT−I)),∇H(T)=logT,
(62)

with the convention 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0 on eigenvalues. This is the convex negative quantum entropy; on trace-one states it differs from the physical entropy by a sign and an additive constant.

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0 define

QOT⁡Cϵ(A,B)=min⁡T⪰0{tr⁡(CT)+ϵH(T):Tr⁡B(T)=A, Tr⁡A(T)=B}.\operatorname{QOT}_C^\epsilon(A,B) = \min_{T\succeq0} \left\{ \operatorname{tr}(CT)+\epsilon H(T): \operatorname{Tr}_B(T)=A,\ \operatorname{Tr}_A(T)=B \right\}.QOTCϵ​(A,B)=T⪰0min​{tr(CT)+ϵH(T):TrB​(T)=A, TrA​(T)=B}.
(63)

This is the non-commutative analogue of entropic OT: the Shannon entropy of a coupling is replaced by the trace entropy of a density matrix Peyré et al., 2019Chakrabarti et al., 2019.

Proposition: Entropic Quantum OT Duality

Assume A≻0A\succ0A≻0, B≻0B\succ0B≻0 and ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0. Then (63) has a unique positive minimizer. Its dual is

QOT⁡Cϵ(A,B)=max⁡F∈Hn, G∈Hm{tr⁡(FA)+tr⁡(GB)−ϵ tr⁡exp⁡ ⁣(F⊗Im+In⊗G−Cϵ)}.\operatorname{QOT}_C^\epsilon(A,B) = \max_{F\in\mathbb H_n,\ G\in\mathbb H_m} \left\{ \operatorname{tr}(FA)+\operatorname{tr}(GB) - \epsilon\, \operatorname{tr} \exp\!\left( \frac{F\otimes I_m+I_n\otimes G-C}{\epsilon} \right) \right\}.QOTCϵ​(A,B)=F∈Hn​, G∈Hm​max​{tr(FA)+tr(GB)−ϵtrexp(ϵF⊗Im​+In​⊗G−C​)}.
(64)

At optimality, primal and dual variables are linked by the Gibbs formula

Te(F,G)=exp⁡ ⁣(F⊗Im+In⊗G−Cϵ).T_e(F,G) = \exp\!\left( \frac{F\otimes I_m+I_n\otimes G-C}{\epsilon} \right).Te​(F,G)=exp(ϵF⊗Im​+In​⊗G−C​).
(65)

with Tr⁡B(Te)=A\operatorname{Tr}_B(T_e)=ATrB​(Te​)=A and Tr⁡A(Te)=B\operatorname{Tr}_A(T_e)=BTrA​(Te​)=B.

Proof

The feasible set is compact and nonempty, and it contains the positive definite point A⊗BA\otimes BA⊗B. The trace entropy is strictly convex on positive semidefinite matrices, hence the regularized primal has a unique minimizer. The minimizer is positive definite: otherwise, moving toward the positive feasible point A⊗BA\otimes BA⊗B would have entropy directional derivative −∞-\infty−∞ at the boundary while changing the linear cost at finite rate. Slater’s condition justifies the Lagrange dual computation. The Fenchel identity

sup⁡T⪰0tr⁡(YT)−ϵH(T)=ϵ tr⁡exp⁡(Y/ϵ)\sup_{T\succeq0} \operatorname{tr}(YT)-\epsilon H(T) = \epsilon\,\operatorname{tr}\exp(Y/\epsilon)T⪰0sup​tr(YT)−ϵH(T)=ϵtrexp(Y/ϵ)
(66)

is the matrix analogue of the scalar exponential conjugacy. Applying it to the Lagrangian with Y=F⊗Im+In⊗G−CY=F\otimes I_m+I_n\otimes G-CY=F⊗Im​+In​⊗G−C gives (64), and the stationarity condition gives (65); differentiating the dual objective with respect to FFF and GGG yields the two marginal equations.

Writing K=exp⁡(−C/ϵ)K=\exp(-C/\epsilon)K=exp(−C/ϵ), the objective differs by a constant from ϵ\epsilonϵ times the quantum KL divergence

DH(T∣K)=tr⁡ ⁣(T(log⁡T−log⁡K)−T+K).D_H(T\mid K) = \operatorname{tr}\!\left( T(\log T-\log K)-T+K \right).DH​(T∣K)=tr(T(logT−logK)−T+K).
(67)

The exact quantum analogue of Sinkhorn is an implicit alternating Bregman projection scheme onto the affine marginal sets

MA={T⪰0:Tr⁡B(T)=A},MB={T⪰0:Tr⁡A(T)=B}.\mathcal M_A=\{T\succeq0:\operatorname{Tr}_B(T)=A\}, \qquad \mathcal M_B=\{T\succeq0:\operatorname{Tr}_A(T)=B\}.MA​={T⪰0:TrB​(T)=A},MB​={T⪰0:TrA​(T)=B}.
(68)
Proposition: Exact Bregman Projections

Assume A,B≻0A,B\succ0A,B≻0 and let K=exp⁡(−C/ϵ)K=\exp(-C/\epsilon)K=exp(−C/ϵ). The minimizer of (63) is equivalently the minimizer of DH(T∣K)D_H(T\mid K)DH​(T∣K) over MA∩MB\mathcal M_A\cap\mathcal M_BMA​∩MB​. Moreover, if a current positive definite matrix has Gibbs form Te(F,G)T_e(F,G)Te​(F,G), then its Bregman projection onto MA\mathcal M_AMA​ has the form Te(F+,G)T_e(F^+,G)Te​(F+,G), where F+F^+F+ is chosen so that Tr⁡BTe(F+,G)=A\operatorname{Tr}_B T_e(F^+,G)=ATrB​Te​(F+,G)=A. The projection onto MB\mathcal M_BMB​ is analogous. Thus, when each one-block marginal equation is solved exactly, alternating Bregman projections are equivalent to alternating block maximization of the dual (64).

Proof

Since log⁡K=−C/ϵ\log K=-C/\epsilonlogK=−C/ϵ,

tr⁡(CT)+ϵH(T)=ϵDH(T∣K)−ϵtr⁡(K).\operatorname{tr}(CT)+\epsilon H(T) = \epsilon D_H(T\mid K)-\epsilon\operatorname{tr}(K).tr(CT)+ϵH(T)=ϵDH​(T∣K)−ϵtr(K).
(69)

For the projection of a positive definite matrix SSS onto MA\mathcal M_AMA​, the affine set contains the positive definite point A⊗Im/mA\otimes I_m/mA⊗Im​/m. The entropy derivative is singular at the boundary, so the projection lies in the interior of the positive cone and the first variation has the form

log⁡T−log⁡S−Λ⊗Im=0,\log T-\log S-\Lambda\otimes I_m=0,logT−logS−Λ⊗Im​=0,
(70)

for a Hermitian multiplier Λ\LambdaΛ. Hence T=exp⁡(log⁡S+Λ⊗Im)T=\exp(\log S+\Lambda\otimes I_m)T=exp(logS+Λ⊗Im​). If S=Te(F,G)S=T_e(F,G)S=Te​(F,G), this is again Te(F+ϵΛ,G)T_e(F+\epsilon\Lambda,G)Te​(F+ϵΛ,G); the multiplier is fixed by the marginal equation. The same argument applies to MB\mathcal M_BMB​. Finally, the first-order optimality condition for maximizing (64) over one block is exactly the corresponding marginal equation, so the Bregman and block-dual views coincide.

In the diagonal case this proposition gives the usual multiplicative Sinkhorn updates. In the non-commutative case, however, the exact block equations

Tr⁡BTe(F,G)=A,Tr⁡ATe(F,G)=B\operatorname{Tr}_B T_e(F,G)=A, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}_A T_e(F,G)=BTrB​Te​(F,G)=A,TrA​Te​(F,G)=B
(71)

do not admit scalar division formulas, because the exponential of F⊗Im+In⊗G−CF\otimes I_m+I_n\otimes G-CF⊗Im​+In​⊗G−C cannot be separated unless the local potential commutes with the cost.

Gurvits Scaling and Quantum Sinkhorn¶

The algorithm often called quantum Sinkhorn comes from the operator-scaling literature of Gurvits and subsequent developments Gurvits, 2003Gurvits, 2004Georgiou & Pavon, 2015Garg & Oliveira, 2018. It replaces the true Gibbs coupling (65) by the symmetric factorization

Ts(F,G)=exp⁡ ⁣(Z2ϵ)exp⁡(−C/ϵ)exp⁡ ⁣(Z2ϵ)=(U⊗V)K(U⊗V),Z=F⊗Im+In⊗G,T_s(F,G) = \exp\!\left(\frac{Z}{2\epsilon}\right) \exp(-C/\epsilon) \exp\!\left(\frac{Z}{2\epsilon}\right) = (U\otimes V)K(U\otimes V), \qquad Z=F\otimes I_m+I_n\otimes G,Ts​(F,G)=exp(2ϵZ​)exp(−C/ϵ)exp(2ϵZ​)=(U⊗V)K(U⊗V),Z=F⊗Im​+In​⊗G,
(72)

where U=exp⁡(F/(2ϵ))U=\exp(F/(2\epsilon))U=exp(F/(2ϵ)), V=exp⁡(G/(2ϵ))V=\exp(G/(2\epsilon))V=exp(G/(2ϵ)) and K=exp⁡(−C/ϵ)K=\exp(-C/\epsilon)K=exp(−C/ϵ). If [Z,C]=0[Z,C]=0[Z,C]=0, then Ts(F,G)=Te(F,G)T_s(F,G)=T_e(F,G)Ts​(F,G)=Te​(F,G); otherwise this is a Strang-type symmetric surrogate.

Fix a Choi convention and let K:Hm→Hn\mathcal K:\mathbb H_m\to\mathbb H_nK:Hm​→Hn​ be the completely positive map represented by the positive Choi matrix KKK; let K⋆\mathcal K^\starK⋆ be its Hilbert--Schmidt adjoint. Up to the transpose dictated by the chosen Choi convention, the marginal equations for the symmetric coupling take the operator-scaling form

U K(V2) U=A,V K⋆(U2) V=B,U\,\mathcal K(V^2)\,U=A, \qquad V\,\mathcal K^\star(U^2)\,V=B,UK(V2)U=A,VK⋆(U2)V=B,
(73)

and can be enforced by the congruence normalizations

RV=K(V2),U←RV−1/2(RV1/2ARV1/2)1/2RV−1/2,SU=K⋆(U2),V←SU−1/2(SU1/2BSU1/2)1/2SU−1/2.\begin{aligned} R_V&=\mathcal K(V^2), & U&\leftarrow R_V^{-1/2} \left(R_V^{1/2} A R_V^{1/2}\right)^{1/2} R_V^{-1/2}, \\ S_U&=\mathcal K^\star(U^2), & V&\leftarrow S_U^{-1/2} \left(S_U^{1/2} B S_U^{1/2}\right)^{1/2} S_U^{-1/2}. \end{aligned}RV​SU​​=K(V2),=K⋆(U2),​UV​←RV−1/2​(RV1/2​ARV1/2​)1/2RV−1/2​,←SU−1/2​(SU1/2​BSU1/2​)1/2SU−1/2​.​
(74)

These inverse square roots are well-defined when K≻0K\succ0K≻0 and U,V,A,B≻0U,V,A,B\succ0U,V,A,B≻0. Under the standard strict-positivity and scalability hypotheses, the alternating normalizations converge to the prescribed marginals Georgiou & Pavon, 2015Garg & Oliveira, 2018. At finite tolerance they return an approximate coupling. When all matrices are diagonal, the updates reduce to classical Sinkhorn scaling; when the targets are proportional to identities, they match the usual bistochastic operator-scaling normalization up to trace convention.

Remark: Gurvits scaling is not the exact Bregman scheme

It is important not to identify (74) with the exact Bregman scheme for (63). The exact Bregman step would enforce the marginals of Te(F,G)=exp⁡((Z−C)/ϵ)T_e(F,G)=\exp((Z-C)/\epsilon)Te​(F,G)=exp((Z−C)/ϵ) and would be a block maximization of the true concave dual (64). Gurvits scaling instead enforces the marginals of the surrogate

Ts=exp⁡ ⁣(Z2ϵ)exp⁡(−C/ϵ)exp⁡ ⁣(Z2ϵ).T_s= \exp\!\left(\frac{Z}{2\epsilon}\right) \exp(-C/\epsilon) \exp\!\left(\frac{Z}{2\epsilon}\right).Ts​=exp(2ϵZ​)exp(−C/ϵ)exp(2ϵZ​).
(75)

The two coincide in the commuting/diagonal regime, but in general the Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff commutator terms do not vanish. The Gurvits iteration should therefore be understood as a tractable symmetric operator-scaling approximation to entropic Q--OT, not as the literal alternating KL projection algorithm.

Remark: Operator-valued couplings

The same definitions extend formally from matrices to separable Hilbert spaces by replacing density matrices with positive trace-class operators of trace one, observables with bounded self-adjoint operators and (57) with partial traces defined by duality against local bounded observables. If Π(A,B)\Pi(A,B)Π(A,B) denotes positive trace-class operators with partial traces AAA and BBB, a bounded cost observable CCC gives the problem inf⁡T∈Π(A,B)Tr⁡(CT)\inf_{T\in\Pi(A,B)}\Tr(CT)infT∈Π(A,B)​Tr(CT). For unbounded positive costs one must define the energy through the quadratic form or spectral truncations, and in the entropic case one must ensure that the Gibbs operator exp⁡(−C/ϵ)\exp(-C/\epsilon)exp(−C/ϵ) is trace class and that the partial traces of the candidate coupling are well-defined. The matrix formulas above are therefore the clean finite-dimensional core; the operator version adds domain and compactness assumptions rather than a different algebraic structure.

Vector, metric-measure and quantum transport extend the same coupling principle in three different directions: richer fibers, unknown cross-space correspondences and non-commutative joint states. Their feasible sets and algorithms differ, but marginal constraints, convex duality and entropy regularization remain the common organizing mechanisms.
